Topic:Unrest, Conflict and War

Sun 14 Jun 2026 at 9:36am

Donald Trump says a peace deal will be signed with Iran on Sunday. (Reuters: Evelyn Hockstein)

Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif says a deal aimed at ending the war in the Middle East is closer than "ever before" and is expected to be finalised within 24 hours.

However, earlier on Saturday, Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei cautioned against commenting on the timing of the signing.

Renewed fighting in Lebanon continues to pose a risk to the deal, with Iran insisting any lasting peace will include an end to fighting between Israel and Iranian proxy groups including Hezbollah.

US President Donald Trump says an initial deal to end the war in the Middle East will be signed on Sunday, a statement backed up by Pakistan's prime minister, though Iran has denied the signing will take place so soon.

Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif said the two sides have agreed on a framework for a peace deal and that Islamabad was preparing for an electronic signing on Sunday, to be followed by technical-level talks next week.

"We are confident that this historic peace deal will form a strong foundation for lasting peace," he said.

Shehbaz Sharif says a deal between the US and Iran is closer than ever before. (Reuters: Maxim Shemetov)

Mr Trump said in a social media post the deal would see Iran immediately open the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway for global oil supplies, which it has largely shut down since February.

However, earlier on Saturday, Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei cautioned against commenting on the timing of the signing.

"We will have to wait and see about the exact date of the signing of the memorandum of understanding, although it will not be tomorrow," state media quoted Mr Baghaei as saying.

"The possibility of this happening in the coming days cannot be ruled out. However, due to the hesitation of the other side, we must be cautious in making any comments about this process."

A US official who spoke to reporters later declined to be drawn on the timing, but said: "It's a great deal and a very strong deal."

It is not the first time the two sides have appeared close to an initial agreement on ending the war, which began on February 28 with joint US-Israeli strikes on Iran, though this time an agreement appears closer than ever before.

The war has sent global energy prices sharply higher and killed thousands of people, mostly in Iran and Lebanon, where the war has revived a conflict between Israel and Iran-aligned Hezbollah militants.

On Friday, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said while changes in the deal were still possible, the tentative agreement showed his country had emerged stronger from the conflict.

Hours after those remarks, US forces shot down multiple Iranian one-way attack drones heading toward the Strait of Hormuz, a source familiar with the matter told Reuters.

Abbas Araqchi says his country emerged stronger from the conflict with the US. (Reuters: Amr Abdallah Dalsh)

The source, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said the drones had posed a threat to commercial traffic.

Iran has for months effectively blockaded the strait, and the US Navy has blocked Iranian ports to reduce its oil exports.

As pro-government rallies continued across Iran, as they have for more than 100 nights, residents and news agencies reported new slogans being chanted by opponents of the agreement with the United States.

A resident in the north-eastern city of Mashhad told Reuters in Dubai that some protesters chanted: "Death to the compromiser" in an apparent reference to Foreign Minister Araqchi.

"Compromiser, resign, resign," the chants continued.

The proposed memorandum of understanding calls for reopening the strait and lifting the US naval blockade, sources on all sides of the talks said.

Negotiations over Iran's nuclear program, Mr Trump's stated rationale for starting the war, would take place afterwards.

Iranians have held nightly rallies against the US and Israel over the past few months. (WANA via Reuters:  Majid Asgaripour)

"Iran is going to open up the Strait of Hormuz, that's a requirement. It could be open with no tolls. As they do that, we will lift our blockade," said the US official who spoke on Saturday.

"It's going to happen in conjunction, and part of the next step, the phase after that, is going to be the de-mining of the straits," the official said, indicating countries in the G7 group of major powers could play a role.

Mr Trump also discussed the efforts to end the Iran conflict in a call with British Prime Minister Keir Starmer, Downing Street said on Saturday.

Draft terms described by multiple sources indicate the US would soon begin releasing billions of dollars in frozen Iranian assets under the deal and waive sanctions on its oil exports, in return for Iran opening the strait.

Iran's Fars news agency quoted Esmaeil Baghaei, the foreign ministry spokesperson, as saying the release of Iran's frozen assets was an integral part of the agreement, and also that Iran would have to charge for services in the Strait of Hormuz.

Amid rising expectations of a pathway to peace between Iran and the US, the reported details of a ceasefire deal appear to show Iran getting numerous concessions from the White House.

Fars also quoted him as saying the presence of foreign military bases in the region must end, without providing details.

Iran's nuclear program would be addressed during a 60-day period of talks as part of the agreement, according to multiple sources.

A US official said the agreement would ultimately lead to the dismantling of Iran's nuclear program, with its stockpile of highly enriched uranium to be destroyed and removed.

But Mr Araqchi said Iran, which sources said has not accepted the dismantling of its nuclear program, wanted to retain the uranium in diluted form.

The proposals also include discussion of possible war reparations for Tehran and dropping longstanding US demands for limits on Iran's missile program, the sources said.

The US official disputed that account.

While the United States and Iran edged closer to a deal, Lebanese state media reported further Israeli strikes had taken place in the country's south, where Israel is fighting the Shia militant group Hezbollah.

The strikes, on Saturday local time, came shortly after the Israeli army issued an "evacuation warning" for 20 locations including the city of Nabatieh ahead of Israeli raids.

The state-run National News Agency (NNA) said Israeli air strikes hit several areas covered by the warning, including the villages of Rihan and Sujud, located not far from Nabatieh.

Smoke billows from southern Lebanon following an Israeli strike, as seen from Nabatieh. (Reuters: Stringer)

The fighting could pose a risk to the peace deal if it continues, with Iran insisting that any deal should encompass an end to fighting involving its supporters and proxies across the region, which includes Hezbollah.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, however, has said Israel will not be part of the peace deal currently being negotiated between the United States and Iran.

Mr Netanyahu has clashed with Mr Trump in recent weeks over US demands that Israel curb its military actions in Lebanon to allow Washington to reach the deal.

Outside the Tehran compound that was home to now-dead Iranian supreme leader Ali Khamenei, hundreds of his supporters gather every night to mourn the only leader many of them have ever known.

Also on Saturday, state media reported the funeral for Iran's late Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei will begin in Tehran on July 4 and conclude with his burial in the north-eastern city of Mashhad on July 9.

Ayatollah Khamenei was killed in Israeli and US strikes on Iran in February.

His death marked the end of more than three decades at the helm of the Islamic republic.

His son, Mojtaba, succeeded him as supreme leader in early March, the third since the establishment of the Islamic republic in 1979.
